title: Blacktop Driveway Sealer: How to Revive Gray, Oxidized Asphalt
h1: Blacktop Driveway Sealer for Gray, Tired Asphalt
query: blacktop driveway sealer for gray, tired asphalt
description: How to tell if faded gray blacktop can still be saved with sealer, which pails suit old porous asphalt, how many to buy, and a two-day DIY plan that holds up.
dek: How to tell if faded gray blacktop can still be saved with sealer, which pails suit old porous asphalt, how many to buy, and a two-day DIY plan that holds up.
intro: A gray blacktop driveway is not a dead driveway. Gray means the top layer of binder has oxidized, which is exactly the problem sealer was invented to fix. The trouble is that old, porous blacktop behaves very differently under a squeegee than the smooth surface on the product photos: it drinks sealer, shows every lap mark and needs more prep. Get the diagnosis right and buy for a thirsty surface, and a weekend of work can buy you several more years.

quickAnswer: Your driveway went from black to gray and the stones are showing. Here is how to tell whether a few pails of sealer will bring it back, and how to do the job so it lasts.

sections.h: Diagnose the Surface Before You Buy Anything

blocks.p: Walk the whole driveway on a dry afternoon with a cup of water and a screwdriver. You are looking for three different conditions, and they need three different responses. Most aging driveways show some of each, so map where they are before deciding what to buy.

Loose stones, sandy grit, rough texture

blocks.p: **Oxidation** is the easy one. Sunlight and oxygen harden the asphalt binder over the years, and the color shifts from black to charcoal to pale gray. The surface feels harder and less tacky on a hot day. A water drop soaks in instead of beading. This is a sealing job, plain and simple.

**Raveling** is the next stage, where the hardened binder stops holding the small particles between stones. You will see loose grit on the surface after rain and individual stones that pop out with a screwdriver tip. Raveled blacktop can still be sealed, but it needs a filled, heavy-bodied product and usually a brushed first coat to push material into the gaps.

**Alligator cracking** is the dealbreaker. A pattern of interlocking cracks, often in wheel paths, means the base underneath has failed and the asphalt is flexing under load. Sealing over it is cosmetic only. Mark those areas, get a patch or replacement quote, and seal the rest of the driveway after the repair.

sections.h: When Gray Blacktop Is Worth Sealing, and When It Is Not

blocks.p: Sealing makes sense when the structure is sound and the problem is mostly on the surface. As a rough guide, if less than about a tenth of the driveway area shows alligator cracking or potholes, repairing those spots and sealing the rest is usually a good use of money. If large areas are breaking up, you are approaching the point where resurfacing or replacement is the honest answer.

Age alone does not decide it. A 25-year-old driveway that was laid on a good base and sealed now and then can be in better shape than a 10-year-old one laid thin on poor fill. Judge by what you see, not by when it was paved. If you are on the fence, our breakdown of [the pros and cons of sealing an asphalt driveway](/sealing-asphalt-driveway-pros-and-cons/) lays out the cases where it pays off.
A USEFUL RULE OF THUMB
Sealer buys time on sound blacktop. It cannot buy back structure.

If you can push a screwdriver into the surface easily, see the base material through cracks, or feel a section flex underfoot, spend your money on repair first. Seal afterward, once the patches have cured.

There is also a real case for sealing a driveway you plan to replace in a few years. A coat of sealer slows raveling and keeps water out of cracks, which can delay that replacement, and it improves curb appeal if you are selling. Just keep expectations in line: you are buying a few seasons, not a new driveway.

One more check: brand-new blacktop is the opposite problem. Fresh asphalt needs time for its oils to cure before sealer will bond, typically six months to a year. If your driveway is new but already looks gray, that is often just surface dust and fines, not oxidation. Our guide on [when to seal a new asphalt driveway](/when-should-you-seal-a-new-asphalt-driveway/) covers how to tell.

sections.h: Choosing a Pail for Old, Porous Blacktop

blocks.p: Old blacktop needs body. A thin, inexpensive maintenance sealer is designed for smooth surfaces that were sealed recently. On gray, open-textured asphalt, it disappears into the voids and leaves a blotchy, brownish finish that needs two or three coats to look even. A filled sealer, which contains fine mineral filler and often sand, sits up on the surface and closes some of that texture on the first coat.

The products we usually point owners of older driveways toward are filled, polymer-modified emulsions like Latex-ite Airport Grade and Jetcoat Premium. Both are water-based, clean up with a hose before curing, and have enough solids to cover texture. Black Jack Drive-Maxx 1000 gives an excellent finish but costs more, and its advantage is largest on smoother surfaces. Budget lines like Henry and Gardner make sense for maintenance coats on driveways in better shape. Our ranked list of the [best asphalt driveway sealers](/best-asphalt-driveway-sealer-reviews/) compares each in detail.

Look at the label for words like filler, crack filling, or rough surfaces, and check the coverage figure. Counterintuitively, a lower coverage number per pail often signals a thicker, more useful product for old blacktop, because the solids have to go somewhere. A pail that promises unusually high coverage is usually thin.

Skip coal tar. It is restricted in Washington, Minnesota and many cities, has a strong odor, irritates skin and eyes during application, and has been linked by U.S. Geological Survey research to elevated levels of harmful compounds in house dust and runoff. Old blacktop does not need it. For a deeper look at what goes into each formula, see our guide to [asphalt sealer chemistry and grades](/best-asphalt-sealer/).

Label coverage figures assume reasonably tight, smooth asphalt. Oxidized and raveled blacktop absorbs considerably more, especially on the first coat. A practical approach is to plan for the first coat at about two-thirds of the label coverage and the second coat at the full label figure.

Here is the math behind that example. At about 200 square feet per pail on the first coat, a 700-square-foot driveway needs three and a half pails, so call it four. At the full 300 on the second coat, it needs between two and three. That makes six or seven pails total, and one more as a buffer. It is much better to bring back an unopened pail than to run out with half the driveway to go.

Buy them all from the same store on the same day and check batch codes if you can. Color can vary slightly between batches, and a mismatch is very visible on a large flat surface. If cost is a concern at those quantities, compare the total against a contractor quote. On larger driveways, bulk pricing can close the gap. Our [driveway sealing cost guide](/how-much-does-it-cost-to-seal-a-driveway/) shows typical figures.

sections.h: The DIY Kit: What to Buy and What to Skip

blocks.p: **For cleaning:** a stiff push broom, a leaf blower if you have one, a garden hose with a jet nozzle or a pressure washer, a driveway degreaser and a stiff scrub brush for oil spots, plus an oil spot primer. An edger or string trimmer handles grass creeping onto the edges.

**For cracks:** a crack filler suited to your crack widths. Pourable fillers work for narrow cracks, while rope-style fillers melted with a propane torch handle medium cracks better. For wide gaps, use backer rod or cold patch. Our roundup of [driveway crack fillers](/best-driveway-crack-filler/) sorts products by width.

**For sealing:** a mixing paddle for a corded drill, a combination squeegee-brush applicator with a long handle, a separate stiff brush for edges, painter's tape and plastic sheeting to protect concrete and siding, old clothes, gloves and safety glasses. Disposable boot covers or cheap shoes you can throw away are worth having.

**What to skip:** paint rollers, which leave a thin, uneven coat and fall apart in filled sealer. Garden sprayers, which clog instantly. And the temptation to dilute sealer with water to make it spread farther. Most labels prohibit it, and it weakens the film. Our guide on [how to seal a driveway](/how-to-seal-a-driveway/) has a printable tool list.

The job splits naturally into a prep day and a sealing day, and it should not be compressed into one. The surface needs to be completely dry after washing, and crack filler needs time to cure before you seal over it. Pick a stretch of at least three dry days with daytime temperatures comfortably above 50 degrees Fahrenheit and nights that stay mild.

blocks.h3: Day one: clean, treat and fill

blocks.p: Trim the edges, sweep and blow off everything loose, and wash the surface thoroughly. On raveled blacktop, use a pressure washer gently or stick to a hose, because aggressive washing pulls out more loose aggregate. Scrub oil spots with degreaser, rinse well, and let them dry. Fill cracks once the surface is dry, following the filler's cure time. Our guide to [removing oil stains from a driveway](/how-to-remove-oil-stains-from-driveway/) covers the tougher spots.

blocks.h3: Day two: prime, mask and seal

blocks.p: Dab oil spot primer on any treated stains and let it dry. Mask the garage floor edge, walkways and anything else you do not want black. Stir each pail thoroughly with the drill paddle. Cut in the edges with a brush, then work in sections from the garage toward the street, so you never need to walk on wet sealer. Apply the first coat in the morning so it has the warm part of the day to dry, then the second in the afternoon once the first is dry to the touch, or the next morning.

Keep an eye on the forecast throughout. A light shower in the first few hours can leave streaks or wash fresh sealer into the street. If you get caught, our page on [rain after driveway sealing](/rain-after-driveway-sealing/) explains how to judge the damage.

sections.h: Getting the First Coat Into Thirsty Blacktop

blocks.p: On old asphalt, the first coat is really a primer. Its job is to fill the open texture and give the second coat a uniform surface to land on. That changes how you apply it.

Use the brush side of your applicator for the first coat, and work it in with a scrubbing motion rather than just spreading it. On raveled spots, go over the area twice. Do not worry if the first coat looks uneven or slightly brown in places. That is the surface absorbing material, and it is why the second coat matters.

On a very hot day, the dry, dark surface can be hot enough to flash-dry sealer before it soaks in. Lightly mist the area with a hose until it is damp but not puddled, then apply. Many labels recommend this, and it helps sealer flow into the pores. Work in the morning or late afternoon on scorching days.

Apply the second coat at right angles to the first, using the squeegee side for a smooth, even finish. This cross-hatching hides lap marks and gives more uniform thickness. Keep a wet edge, and do not go back over areas that have started to set, which leaves visible drag marks. Two thin coats always beat one heavy coat, which skins over, stays soft underneath and tends to crack.

sections.h: After the Coat: Curing, Cleanup and the Next Three Years

blocks.p: Block the driveway with sawhorses, trash cans or tape across the entrance so delivery drivers and visitors do not drive on it. Most labels call for 24 to 48 hours before vehicle traffic, and longer in cool, humid or shaded conditions. Foot traffic is usually fine once it is dry to the touch, often after several hours. Our guide on [how long driveway sealer takes to dry](/how-long-for-driveway-sealer-to-dry/) covers the variables.

Clean tools with water before the sealer sets. Once cured, it takes mineral spirits or a citrus cleaner to remove. Splatters on concrete come off far more easily within minutes than the next day, so keep a bucket of water and a scrub brush nearby while you work.

For the first week or two, avoid turning the steering wheel while the car is not moving, and be careful with kickstands, trailer jacks and lawn furniture. Fresh sealer is soft and will dent and scuff until it fully hardens.

Then leave it alone. Old blacktop sealed properly with two filled coats typically needs another coat in about two to three years, not every year. Use the water test each spring: when water stops beading and starts soaking in, it is time. Sealing too often builds a thick layer that cracks and flakes. Our guide on [how often to seal a driveway](/how-often-should-you-seal-your-driveway/) explains how to read the surface. And if you have a mix of asphalt and concrete surfaces around the house, our guide to [choosing a driveway sealer by surface](/best-driveway-sealer/) covers the concrete side.

mistakes: Buying a thin sealer for a porous surface

A low-cost maintenance sealer that promises high coverage is designed for smooth, recently sealed asphalt. On gray, raveled blacktop it soaks in, looks blotchy and needs extra coats. The cheaper pail ends up costing more. Choose a filled product, and expect lower coverage per pail on the first coat.
Pressure washing raveled asphalt too hard

A narrow, powerful pressure-washer jet strips loose stones and fines from aged blacktop, leaving a rougher surface that absorbs even more sealer. Use a wide fan tip, keep it moving and stand back, or simply use a hose and stiff broom. The goal is clean, not blasted.

A web of interconnected cracks means the base has failed. Sealer hides it for a few months, then the cracks reappear and spread. Mark those areas, get them patched or replaced, and seal the rest of the driveway after the repairs cure. Otherwise you are paying to cover up a problem that keeps growing.

Diluting sealer to make it go further is tempting when you need seven pails. Most labels prohibit it, and it weakens the film, cuts water resistance and shortens the coat's life. If the product is too thick to spread, mist the pavement or use the brush side of your applicator instead.

Delivery drivers, guests and neighbors turning around will drive straight onto fresh sealer unless physically blocked. Tire tracks in a new coat are hard to fix without another coat. Block the entrance with something solid and visible for at least two days, and tell anyone expecting to visit.
bottomLine: Gray blacktop is usually a surface problem, and surface problems are what sealer fixes. Diagnose first: oxidation and light raveling are worth sealing, while alligator cracking and potholes need repair before any sealer goes down. Then buy a filled product, plan for more pails than the label suggests, and give yourself two dry days. Brush the first coat in, squeegee the second across it, keep cars off for two days, and do not reseal again until the water test says so. Done that way, a few hundred dollars and a weekend of work can keep an aging driveway in service for years longer than it would last untouched.

faqs.q: Is blacktop sealer different from asphalt sealer?
faqs.a: No. Blacktop is simply another name for asphalt pavement, more common in some regions. Products labeled blacktop sealer and asphalt driveway sealer are the same category: usually a water-based asphalt emulsion, sometimes with filler, sand or polymer added. What matters is the formula and how much filler it carries, not which of the two names is on the pail.

faqs.q: Can sealer make a gray driveway black again?
faqs.a: Yes, on the surface. Sealer restores the black color by adding a fresh layer of asphalt-based material over the oxidized binder. On very porous blacktop, the first coat may look uneven or slightly brown as it soaks in, so plan for two coats. The color fades again over a few years as the sealer itself oxidizes.

faqs.q: How much sealer does an old driveway need?
faqs.a: More than the label suggests. Porous, oxidized blacktop can absorb noticeably more sealer on the first coat. A practical plan is to assume about two-thirds of the stated coverage for the first coat and the full figure for the second, then add a spare pail. Unopened pails can be returned or stored above freezing for the next job.

faqs.q: Should I brush or squeegee sealer on old blacktop?
faqs.a: Both. A stiff brush works the first coat into open, rough texture and fills the gaps between stones. A squeegee gives the second coat a smoother, more even finish. Many combination tools have a brush on one side and a squeegee on the other, which makes switching easy. Use a separate brush for edges and corners.

faqs.q: Can I seal blacktop that has loose stones?
faqs.a: Yes, if the base is sound. Loose stones and grit are signs of raveling, which a filled sealer can slow down. Sweep away everything loose first, avoid aggressive pressure washing, and brush the first coat in to bind the remaining fines. If stones keep popping out in large areas or the surface feels soft, get a repair quote first.

faqs.q: Is it worth sealing a driveway I plan to replace?
faqs.a: Often, yes. Sealing slows raveling and keeps water out of cracks, which can extend the driveway's life by a few years and push back the cost of replacement. It also improves appearance if you are selling the house. It is not worth it if large areas already show alligator cracking or potholes, because the money is better put toward the replacement.

faqs.q: What temperature do I need for sealing blacktop?
faqs.a: Most water-based sealers call for air and surface temperatures of at least 50 degrees Fahrenheit and rising, with nights that stay above that through the cure. Some ask for 55. Very hot pavement can flash-dry sealer before it bonds, so mist the surface or work in cooler parts of the day. Our temperature guide covers regional timing in detail.
